# Instruments: make your own from recordings (`yinse:`)

Turn a set of single-note recordings into a small instrument muser plays like a built-in one. muser measures each note's
partials (frequency, starting level, a fast and a slow decay, the beating between the strings of a course, left/right
level and phase) and its attack noise, and how much the other strings ring along. The result is a JSON of numbers
(about 150 KB for 40 notes), not audio. It suits sounds that are struck or plucked and ring away by themselves:
yangqin, guzheng, piano, harp, bells, mallets. Not blown or bowed sounds that are held.

```bash
muser yinse extract ~/samples/yangqin/ -o yangqin.yinse.json --name "my yangqin"
muser yinse compare yangqin.yinse.json ~/samples/yangqin/      # how close it is, note by note
```

```json
{ "instrument": "yinse:yangqin.yinse.json" }
```

From an instrument muser can already play (an SFZ library you may use, a plugin, a built-in one), let muser play the notes itself:

```bash
muser yinse extract --from "sfz:Piano.sfz" --pitches 21-108/3 --velocities 0.3,0.6,0.9 --hold 6 -o piano.yinse.json --notes-dir piano-notes
muser yinse compare piano.yinse.json piano-notes/
```

`--from` also plays a short note per pitch to measure the dampers: a piano's notes then stop when released (the sustain pedal holds them), a yangqin's ring on.
Check the source's license before you share what you extract (see the library rules below).

## Libraries

Extracted instruments can live in a library such as [muser-yinse](https://github.com/claw-works/muser-yinse): put its folder
on `MUSER_YINSE_PATH` (several with the path separator) and write `yinse:<family>/<name>`, e.g. `yinse:strike/yangqin`, which
finds `instruments/strike/yangqin/yangqin.yinse.json` there. A plain file path works too.

## Recordings

- One note per file (wav, flac, aiff, ogg or mp3), starting at the attack, ringing until it has died away (at least 2-3 s).
  Dry is best: reverb in the recording ends up in the decays.
- Pitch from the file name (`A4`, `Eb3`, `C#5`, `Cs5`, or a MIDI number such as `69`), otherwise it is measured from the sound.
- Velocity from the file name (`v80` and `vel100` on 0-127, `v0.7`, or `pp p mp mf f ff`); otherwise the files of one pitch are
  ordered from soft to loud. One recording every 3-5 semitones and 2-3 velocities is enough: notes in between are blended
  from the nearest recorded pitches and velocities.

## Articulations (演奏法)

Tag recordings in the file name and they become playing techniques of the instrument; a note picks one with
`"articulation": "<name>"`. `muser instruments yinse:<file>` lists what an instrument has; a name it lacks fails validation.

- **Sounds**: `mute` (闷音, `muted` too), `harmonic`, `back` (反竹), `pluck`, `staccato`, `rim`, `soft`, `hard`, or any name as
  `art-<name>` (`A4_art-fanzhu_v90.wav`). Each gets its own partial tables from its own recordings (a few pitches are enough;
  pitches in between blend as usual).
- **Gestures**, measured from one or more recordings and applied to the plain sound:
  - `tremolo` (轮音): a recording of a tremolo gives strokes per second, how loud the other hammer is, and whether it speeds up.
    Then `"articulation": "tremolo"` (or `"tremolo": true`) plays every tremolo that way.
  - `vibrato` (揉音): a recording of a note with vibrato gives its depth (cents), rate and delay; `"articulation": "vibrato"` on a note.
  - `damp` (止音): a note struck and then stopped gives how fast it is stopped; `"articulation": "damp"` (or `"damp": true`).
  Gesture recordings are only measured, never used as sounds, so the instrument also needs plain notes.

```text
A4_v80.wav  A4_v80_mute.wav  D5_tremolo.wav  A4_vibrato.wav  E4_damp.wav
```

## Playing it

- Notes ring on after they end (no dampers); set `"release": 0.3` in `instrument_params` to damp them.
- `"tremolo": true` on a note plays it as a tremolo (`tremolo_rate` strokes a second); `bend` works on every note.
- It is not level-calibrated: it plays as loud as the recordings. Check with `muser mix-report`.
- `compare` plays every recording's pitch and velocity on the extracted instrument and prints the spectral difference
  (third-octave bands, first 2 s, loudness matched; around 2-3 dB is close), the decay at 0.1 / 0.5 / 1 / 2 s and the stereo
  correlation, beside the recording's.
